## Exponential Smoothing (ETS)

*Idea*: Take all future forecasts as a weighted average of all observations with geometric weights biased towards more recent observations: $\hat y_{t+h} = \alpha y_t + \alpha (1-\alpha)y_{t-1} + \alpha (1-\alpha)^2y_{t-2}\dots$ where $0 < \alpha \le 1$. This creates the **level**. Then add trend and seasonality components

**Trend**: There are two choices for this component: 

- *Additive*: the final trend (slope) is determined by a weighted average of all the slopes in the data, then that is assumed to be the slope for all future points
- *Additive damped*: The slope at time $t+h$ is forecasted to be $\phi + \phi^2 + \dots + \phi^h$ where $0 < \phi \le 1$ (but in practice, $0.8 \le \phi \le 0.98$)

**Seasonality**: There are two choices for this component:

- *Additive*: The seasonal effect is constant and added to the level
- *Multiplicative*: The seasonal effect is proportional to the level and multiplied to the level + trend

## ARIMA

*Idea*: Autoregressive and moving average models can be used to model a stationary time series. A non-stationary time series can be made stationary by differencing it.

ARIMA$(p, d, q)$ is a regression model that combines $AR(p)$ and $MA(q)$ and differences the data $d$ times

**Seasonality**: SARIMA$(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)_m$ includes a seasonal component relating observations to that of the last season instead of the last observation. E.g. $P = 1$ means values in March are autoregressed on values in last March, $D=1$ performs a seasonal difference

**ARIMAX**: Can use covariates ($x$ regressors). Instead of $y_t$ being modeled as an ARIMA process, we have e.g. $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{1,t} + \nu_t$ where error $\nu_t$ is an ARIMA process. Note that all variables have to be stationary, usually done by differencing them all the same amount.
